questions.question: A 10-day-old has a rectal temperature of 38.1°C but looks comfortable. What is the safest disposition?
choices: Give an antipyretic and recheck tomorrow
Arrange emergency evaluation under a young-infant fever pathway
Observe at home if feeding continues
Repeat the temperature after the next feeding
questions.explanation: A documented rectal temperature of 38.0°C or higher in a young infant requires urgent age-specific evaluation even when the infant appears well at one moment.

questions.question: Which approach best assesses jaundice in a four-day-old infant?
choices: Use skin color alone
Wait until jaundice reaches the legs
Interpret an objective bilirubin by age in hours, gestational age, trend, feeding, and risk factors
Use birth weight as the only risk factor
questions.explanation: Bilirubin management is time- and risk-dependent. Objective measurement, age in hours, gestation, trend, neurotoxicity risks, feeding, and clinical status guide action.

questions.question: Which finding most strongly supports effective feeding in a newborn?
choices: Frequent feeds plus audible swallowing, improving output, satiety, and an appropriate weight trajectory
A feed lasting exactly 20 minutes
Parent breast fullness
The infant sleeping through every feed
questions.explanation: Feeding adequacy is a pattern of transfer, hydration, output, behavior, and serial weight. Frequency or duration alone cannot prove intake.

questions.question: A newborn did not pass the initial hearing screen. Which action is most appropriate?
choices: Document normal hearing if the infant startles
Wait until school entry
Explain that the screen is diagnostic of hearing loss
Arrange the specified repeat or diagnostic pathway and track the result to completion
questions.explanation: A failed screen is not a diagnosis, but it requires timely follow-up with explicit ownership and closed-loop result tracking.

questions.question: Which sleep plan best matches current infant safe-sleep guidance?
choices: Prone sleep with a positioner
Supine sleep on a firm, flat, separate approved surface without soft objects
A car seat for routine overnight sleep
Bed sharing when a caregiver is very tired
questions.explanation: Infants should be placed supine on a firm, flat, noninclined separate sleep surface without loose bedding or soft objects; room sharing is preferred over bed sharing.

questions.question: Which newborn finding requires emergency evaluation?
choices: Brief hiccups after feeding
Peeling skin on the ankles
Bilious green vomiting
A single sneeze
questions.explanation: Bilious emesis can indicate intestinal obstruction or volvulus and requires emergency evaluation rather than routine feeding advice.

questions.question: Why should femoral pulses be assessed during the newborn examination?
choices: They help identify impaired lower-body perfusion that may signal critical left-sided obstructive heart disease
They diagnose all murmurs
They replace pulse-oximetry screening
They determine gestational age
questions.explanation: Weak or delayed femoral pulses can be an important clue to aortic arch obstruction, although pulse examination does not replace the broader cardiac assessment.

questions.question: A newborn has frequent feeds but remains sleepy, has scant urine, and continues to lose weight. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Frequency proves adequate intake
Sleepiness is always normal in the first week
The infant only needs a longer interval between feeds
Ineffective transfer or illness must be assessed promptly
questions.explanation: Frequent feeding can coexist with inadequate transfer. Sleepiness, low output, and an adverse weight trend require prompt evaluation of hydration, jaundice, illness, and feeding.

questions.question: Which is the best method for preventing a missed newborn screening result?
choices: Tell the family to call if worried
Assign an owner, deadline, result route, and documented next action
Assume the birth hospital will manage it
Wait until the two-month visit
questions.explanation: Closed-loop care identifies who owns the result, when it is due, how it returns, and what happens if it is abnormal or missing.

questions.question: A postpartum caregiver reports hearing voices commanding harm to the infant. What should the FNP do?
choices: Provide emergency psychiatric and infant-safety intervention
Offer a routine depression screen at the next visit
Focus only on the newborn examination
Recommend more sleep without escalation
questions.explanation: Command hallucinations involving harm represent an immediate psychiatric and infant-safety emergency requiring urgent coordinated intervention.
